description_full: American Electric Power Company, Inc., an electric public utility holding company, engages in the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity for sale to retail and wholesale customers in the United States. It operates through Vertically Integrated Utilities, Transmission and Distribution Utilities, AEP Transmission Holdco, and Generation & Marketing segments. The company generates electricity using coal and lignite, nuclear, natural gas, renewable, hydro, solar, wind, and other energy sources; owns, operates, maintains, and invests in transmission infrastructure; and engages in the retail supply, and wholesale energy trading and marketing businesses. It operates approximately 252,000 circuit miles of distribution lines; 38,000 circuit miles of transmission lines; and 25,000 MWs of regulated owned generating capacity. American Electric Power Company, Inc. was incorporated in 1906 and is headquartered in Columbus, Ohio.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 17K people. Revenue per employee of $1.2M ranks in the above the sector median among Utilities peers. Each employee generates $199K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $3K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: American Electric Power Company is a large-cap utilities business with a $70.3B market cap on $21.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $3.5B in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.94× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.0) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Above-average short interest at 5.0% of float
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

sector_tailwinds: Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
63 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 6% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.

val: The stock trades only 12% below its DCF fair value of $147, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $101 to $216 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 5.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.2% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.14).

Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.94x.
ROE of 11% is amplified by 3.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

The current ratio of 0.45 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.7% over 3 years, 8.0% over 5 years and 2.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 2% of profits supports about 0.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -1.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 12%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 15.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 24, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 98%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (3.0% in dividends, less 1.1% of net share issuance).
The share count has grown 1.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 63 consecutive years, raising it 7.1% a year over the last five.
